subject: Engelska
title: Grammar: comparison and adverbs
sourceSummary: Comparing adjectives with -er/-est or more/most, the irregular forms good/better/best and bad/worse/worst, and the difference between adjectives and adverbs. Here you also practise comparisons with as ... as and than.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: "My bike is ___ than yours."
questions.opener: Short adjectives (one syllable) are compared with -er, not with "more".
questions.explanation: "Fast" has only one syllable and is compared with -er: faster. "More fast" is wrong because "more" is used for longer adjectives, and "more faster" is double comparison.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: "This is the ___ film I have ever seen."
questions.opener: Long adjectives (three syllables or more) take most in the superlative.
questions.explanation: "Interesting" is long and is compared with more/most: the most interesting. "More interesting" is comparative and means "more interesting" in a comparison of two, but here the superlative is required after "the".

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: "The weather today is ___ than yesterday — it's raining and freezing."
questions.opener: "Bad" doesn't follow the -er pattern but has its own completely different form.
questions.explanation: "Bad" is compared irregularly: bad – worse – worst. "Worst" is superlative and can't be used together with "than", which always goes with the comparative.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word: "He speaks English very ___."
questions.opener: Does the word describe the noun "English", or how he speaks?
questions.explanation: The word describes how he speaks, that is, the verb — so the adverb "well" is used. "Good" is an adjective and describes nouns: "His English is good."

questions.opener: Adverbs are usually formed from the adjective + -ly and describe how something is done.
choices: She answered the question quick and correct.
She answered the question quickly and correctly.
She answered quickly the question correct.
She quick answered the question correctly.
questions.explanation: The words describe how she answered, so the adverb forms quickly and correctly are used. "Quick" and "correct" are adjectives and would describe a noun, for example "a quick answer".

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: "My sister is ___ me — we are both 165 cm."
questions.opener: When the degree is equal, a fixed construction with two small words around the adjective is used.
questions.explanation: Equal degree is expressed with as + the base form of the adjective + as: "as tall as me". "Than" is only used after a comparative, for example "taller than me".

questions.prompt: Correct the four errors: "My new phone is more better than my old one. It is the expensivest phone in the shop, but the camera works very good and it starts more quick."
questions.opener: Look for double comparison, an incorrect superlative form, and an adjective that should be an adverb.
questions.answer: My new phone is better than my old one. It is the most expensive phone in the shop, but the camera works very well and it starts more quickly.
steps: "more better" → "better". "Good" is compared irregularly to better, and you never combine "more" with an -er form.
"the expensivest" → "the most expensive". Adjectives with three syllables take most in the superlative, not -est.
"works very good" → "works very well". The word describes how the camera works, so the adverb well is needed.
"starts more quick" → "starts more quickly". The adverb of quick is quickly, and it's the adverb form that is compared here.

questions.prompt: How are adjectives compared in English, and when are adverbs used instead of adjectives?
questions.answer: Short adjectives (1 syllable, often also 2 ending in -y): -er/-est — old/older/oldest · easy/easier/easiest (y becomes i) · big/bigger/biggest (double consonant) · Long adjectives (2–3+ syllables): more/most — more careful/most careful · Irregular: good/better/best · bad/worse/worst · much–many/more/most · little/less/least · far/further/furthest · Never double comparison: "more better" and "most easiest" are wrong · Comparative + than (taller than me) · equal degree: as + base form + as (as tall as me) · Adjectives describe nouns (a quick car, her English is good) · Adverbs describe verbs and are usually formed with -ly (drives quickly, speaks well) · Remember: good → the adverb well.
